questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Svea Tech AB, a Swedish software company without an SEC license in the Philippines, appointed Manila Data Solutions Inc. as its exclusive Philippine reseller. Under their agreement, Manila Data purchases software licenses from Svea Tech, resells them to local clients under its own corporate name, determines its own retail prices, and assumes all credit risks. Separately, Svea Tech entered into a direct agreement with Luzon Logistics Corp. to design and install an automated warehouse tracking platform in Laguna. Svea Tech engineers spent eight months working on site in Laguna to complete the project. Luzon Logistics accepted the completed platform and paid forty percent of the contract price, but subsequently refused to settle the remaining balance, claiming Svea Tech lacks legal capacity to sue due to its unlicensed status. Svea Tech filed a collection lawsuit against Luzon Logistics in the Regional Trial Court. Decide whether Svea Tech was doing business through (a) the reseller agreement and (b) the direct project contract, and whether its lawsuit against Luzon Logistics should be dismissed.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Svea Tech was not doing business through the reseller agreement, but it was doing business through the direct project contract. However, its collection lawsuit against Luzon Logistics should not be dismissed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the Foreign Investments Act, appointing an independent distributor in the Philippines that trades in its own name and for its own account is explicitly excluded from the definition of doing business. Conversely, executing a service contract that directly fulfills the principal commercial object of a foreign entity within the country constitutes doing business. Although an unlicensed foreign entity engaged in business cannot maintain court actions, a domestic contracting party that accepted performance and reaped benefits is legally barred under the doctrine of estoppel from challenging the foreign entity's capacity to sue.
suggestedAnswer.application: Regarding the reseller, Manila Data bought licenses, set its own prices, and bore all credit risk for its own account, placing the arrangement squarely under the statutory exclusion. Regarding the project contract, Svea Tech performed its core technical operations in Laguna for eight months, showing continuous prosecution of its commercial purpose. Nonetheless, because Luzon Logistics contracted directly with Svea Tech, accepted the operational system, paid partial consideration, and continues to utilize the platform, it cannot invoke Svea Tech's lack of license to evade its financial obligation.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Svea Tech engaged in business solely via the direct project contract. Nevertheless, Luzon Logistics is estopped from asserting Svea Tech's lack of license, allowing the collection lawsuit to proceed.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 7042, Sec. 3(d); Steelcase, Inc. v. Design International Selections, Inc., G.R. No. 171995, April 18, 2012; Magna Ready Mix Concrete Corp. v. Andersen Bjornstad Kane Jacobs, Inc., G.R. No. 196158, January 20, 2021. Checked against the official text: https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1991/06/13/republic-act-no-7042/, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2012/apr2012/gr_171995_2012.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2021/jan2021/gr_196158_2021.html.

The appointment violates the Anti-Dummy Law. Under Section 2-A, the president, managers or persons in charge of the corporation are criminally liable, and the right, franchise or business enjoyed in violation of the law may be forfeited.

The SEC or DTI will order the company to restrict domestic sales to forty percent or less. Continued non-compliance will lead to cancellation of its corporate registration.

How should corporate nationality be determined in this case?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Under the Control Test, Apex Mining Corp. is deemed a Philippine national. However, if doubt exists regarding the genuine ownership due to corporate layering or foreign financing, the Grandfather Rule applies as a secondary test.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the Foreign Investments Act and Supreme Court doctrine in Narra Nickel, the Control Test is the primary rule for determining corporate nationality: if a corporate shareholder is at least sixty percent Filipino-owned, its entire shareholding is counted as Filipino. However, when doubt arises as to the true percentage of Filipino equity, the Grandfather Rule applies to trace actual indirect beneficial ownership.
suggestedAnswer.application: Applying the Control Test, HoldCo Inc. is sixty percent Filipino-owned, making it a Philippine national whose entire sixty percent interest in Apex counts as Filipino. Thus, Apex satisfies the sixty percent requirement on paper. Nevertheless, because corporate layering is present, if evidence shows that Canadian capital funded the Filipino holdings, the Grandfather Rule will be applied, yielding only thirty-six percent actual Filipino equity (60% x 60%), disqualifying Apex.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The Control Test applies initially to establish Filipino nationality, but if corporate layering or foreign control is shown to create doubt, the Grandfather Rule applies to disqualify the entity.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 7042, Sec. 3(a); Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp., G.R. No. 195580, April 21, 2014. Grandfather Rule mathematically traces actual equity across corporate tiers

questions.prompt: Dr. Aris developed a surgical method for spinal fusion that reduces recovery time by half. Alongside this procedure, he designed a specialized titanium spinal implant specifically engineered to execute the fusion. Dr. Aris filed patent applications for both the surgical procedure and the titanium implant. The Intellectual Property Office denied the application for the surgical method but admitted the application for the implant. Is the IPO's action legally sound?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, the action of the Intellectual Property Office is legally sound.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 22.3 of Republic Act No. 8293 (Intellectual Property Code), methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy, and diagnostic methods practiced on the human or animal body, are non-patentable. However, the law explicitly provides that this prohibition does not apply to products and compositions for use in any of these methods.
suggestedAnswer.application: Here, Dr. Aris' surgical method for spinal fusion constitutes a method of surgical treatment of the human body, placing it squarely within non-patentable subject matter. Conversely, the specialized titanium spinal implant is a physical product designed for use in surgical treatment, which falls outside the exclusion.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Therefore, the IPO correctly rejected the surgical method application while admitting the application for the titanium implant.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 22.3 (Sec. 22 as amended by R.A. No. 9502 leaves 22.3 unchanged). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2008/ra_9502_2008.html.

keyPoints: Surgical methods for treating the human body are non-patentable under Section 22.3 of R.A. 8293.
The statutory exclusion from patentability does not extend to products or devices used in surgical methods.
The specialized titanium implant is a patentable product, whereas the surgical procedure itself is excluded.

questions.prompt: Vince, a senior software developer at TechCorp, was assigned as part of his regular duties to create an inventory tracking application. While working on the software during office hours, Vince independently conceived and designed a novel cryptographic algorithm for secure file transfer—a project completely outside his assigned work duties. Vince used TechCorp's computers and servers to test his cryptographic algorithm. Who owns the right to the patent over the cryptographic algorithm?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The right to the patent belongs to Vince, the employee.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 30.2(a) of R.A. 8293, an invention made by an employee in the course of his employment contract belongs to the employee if the inventive activity is not part of his regular duties, even if the employee uses the time, facilities, and materials of the employer.
suggestedAnswer.application: In this case, Vince's regular duties involved building inventory tracking applications. The conception of the cryptographic algorithm was entirely outside his assigned regular duties. The mere fact that he utilized TechCorp's office hours, computers, and servers does not vest ownership of the patent in TechCorp.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Thus, Vince owns the right to the patent over the cryptographic algorithm.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 30.2. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Inventions outside regular duties belong to the employee under Section 30.2(a) of R.A. 8293.
Employee's use of employer's time, facilities, and materials does not shift patent ownership to the employer if inventive activity is not part of regular duties.
Employer owns inventions under Section 30.2(b) only when the invention results from the performance of regularly-assigned duties.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Global Pharma filed a patent application in Japan for a new anti-inflammatory compound on February 10, 2024. On November 15, 2024, Global Pharma filed a patent application for the exact same compound with the Philippine IPO, expressly claiming priority based on the Japanese filing, and submitted certified copies in English on January 10, 2025. Meanwhile, Local Labs filed a Philippine patent application for the identical compound on June 1, 2024. Local Labs contends it has the prior right under the first-to-file rule because its Philippine filing preceded Global Pharma's actual Philippine submission. Resolve the dispute.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Global Pharma has the prior right to the patent over the compound.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 31 of R.A. 8293, an application for a patent filed by a person who has previously applied for the same invention in another country which by treaty, convention, or law affords similar privileges to Filipino citizens shall be considered as filed as of the date of filing the foreign application, provided that: (a) priority is expressly claimed; (b) the local application is filed within 12 months from the earliest foreign filing date; and (c) a certified copy of the foreign application together with an English translation is filed within 6 months from the Philippine filing. A right of priority matters only when there are two or more conflicting applications for the same invention (E.I. Dupont De Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco).
suggestedAnswer.application: Global Pharma satisfied all three requisites: it expressly claimed priority, filed in the Philippines within 9 months (well within the 12-month window), and submitted the certified copy with its English translation within 2 months of local filing (well within 6 months). Consequently, Global Pharma's filing date retroacts to February 10, 2024, preceding Local Labs' June 1, 2024 filing.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Global Pharma's right of priority prevails over Local Labs' local application.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 29 and 31; E.I. Dupont De Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, G.R. No. 174379, August 31, 2016. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2016/aug2016/gr_174379_2016.html.

keyPoints: Right of priority under Section 31 of R.A. 8293 accords the effective filing date of the earliest foreign application.
Requisites: express claim of priority, local filing within 12 months, and certified translation within 6 months.
Timely compliance retroacts the priority date, defeating subsequent local filings under the first-to-file system.
questions.correction: Correction: The legal basis now follows Sec. 31's exact requirements: the earlier application must be in a country that gives Filipinos similar privileges, and what must be filed within six months is a certified copy of the foreign application together with an English translation (NotebookLM said "a certified copy ... in English"). A line from E.I. Dupont De Nemours v. Director Francisco (priority matters only when applications conflict) was added, and its title corrected. Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 31, and G.R. No. 174379.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Since 2021, Craft Brewery has been commercially manufacturing and selling an organic filtration system in Cebu in good faith without obtaining a patent. In 2023, Mega Tech independently invented the exact same filtration system and secured a Philippine patent under the first-to-file rule. In 2024, Mega Tech sued Craft Brewery for patent infringement. Craft Brewery invokes the prior user rule as a defense. Furthermore, Craft Brewery wants to sell its entire brewery business, including the right to use the filtration system, to North Drinks. Can Craft Brewery raise the prior user defense, and can the right be assigned to North Drinks?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, Craft Brewery can validly invoke the prior user defense, and it can assign the right to North Drinks provided the transfer includes its entire business enterprise.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 73 of R.A. 8293, any prior user who in good faith was using the invention in the Philippines before the filing or priority date of the patent application has the right to continue such use. Section 73 further dictates that this right of a prior user may only be transferred or assigned together with his enterprise or business, or with that part of his business in which the use or preparation was made.
suggestedAnswer.application: Craft Brewery used the filtration system in good faith prior to Mega Tech's patent application, insulating it from infringement liability. Moreover, because Craft Brewery is selling its entire brewery business to North Drinks, the prior user right validly transfers to North Drinks along with the enterprise.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Craft Brewery is not liable for patent infringement, and the prior user right can be validly transferred to North Drinks as part of the sale of the business.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 73. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Good-faith prior user before filing/priority date is protected from infringement actions under Section 73 of R.A. 8293.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: AgriCorp owns a patent for a motorized grain thresher. The patent claim explicitly specifies a three-stage mechanical rotary blade assembly driven by a belt system. BioTech produced a competing grain thresher that replaces the belt drive with a high-torque hydraulic drive mechanism. While the hydraulic drive performs the same function of rotating the blades to separate grain and yields identical output, it operates through a fundamentally distinct fluid-pressure mechanism rather than mechanical belt tension. AgriCorp sued BioTech for patent infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. Will the suit prosper?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, AgriCorp's patent infringement suit will not prosper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the Doctrine of Equivalents, patent infringement occurs when an accused device performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result (the Function-Means-Result test). As held in Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 126627), identity of result alone does not constitute infringement unless the accused product operates by substantially the same means or mode of operation.
suggestedAnswer.application: While BioTech's thresher achieves the same result and performs the same function of separating grain, it does so using a hydraulic drive mechanism, which is a fundamentally different means compared to AgriCorp's mechanical belt-driven system. Thus, the 'means' element of the function-means-result test is unsatisfied.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Consequently, AgriCorp failed to establish infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 75.2; Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 126627, August 14, 2003. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2003/aug2003/gr_126627_2003.html.

keyPoints: Doctrine of Equivalents requires satisfaction of all three prongs: function, means, and result.
Identity of function and result is insufficient if the accused device operates through a substantially different means.
Failure to prove substantial identity of means defeats a claim under the doctrine of equivalents.

In 2020, Zenith Foods filed an application with the IPO for the registration of 'SUNRISE' for packaged baked goods. Zenith acted in good faith, and the IPO issued a certificate of registration in 2021. In 2023, Zenith demanded that Apex cease using 'SUNRISE'. Apex refused, arguing it was the first user and true owner of the mark. Who has the superior right to the trademark 'SUNRISE'?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Zenith Foods has the superior right to the trademark 'SUNRISE'.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 122 of R.A. 8293, rights in a mark are acquired solely through registration validly made in accordance with the law. In Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc. (G.R. No. 211850), the Supreme Court clarified that prior use is no longer a condition for acquiring trademark ownership, and the first-to-file/register system governs.
suggestedAnswer.application: Zenith validly registered the mark 'SUNRISE' with the IPO in good faith. Apex's prior commercial use since 2015 without registration does not grant it ownership of the trademark. Although Apex may continue as a prior user in good faith under Section 159.1, ownership and exclusive rights to the mark belong to Zenith.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Zenith Foods holds superior rights as the registered trademark owner.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 122 and 159.1; Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc., G.R. No. 211850, September 8, 2020. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2020/sep2020/gr_211850_2020.html.

keyPoints: Trademark rights under R.A. 8293, Section 122 are acquired solely through registration, not prior use.
Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm reaffirmed that the Philippines strictly adheres to the first-to-file rule.
Unregistered prior users do not acquire trademark ownership over a later good-faith registrant.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: FreshBites Inc. filed a trademark application for 'CRISP' on March 1, 2020, and the registration was granted on August 15, 2021. Due to severe cash flow shortages and lack of operating funds, FreshBites failed to file its Declaration of Actual Use (DAU) within three years from the filing date. In April 2023, the IPO Director of Trademarks issued an order removing 'CRISP' from the register. FreshBites appealed, claiming that financial constraints constitute a valid excuse for non-use. Is FreshBites' position correct?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, FreshBites' position is incorrect.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 124.2 of R.A. 8293, failure to file a Declaration of Actual Use (DAU) within 3 years from the filing date results in the refusal of the application or the removal of the mark from the Register by the Director. (A separate declaration is due within one year from the fifth anniversary of the registration under Section 145.) Furthermore, Section 152.1 explicitly provides that while non-use may be excused if caused by circumstances arising independently of the will of the owner, lack of funds shall not excuse non-use of a mark.
suggestedAnswer.application: FreshBites failed to submit its 3-year DAU within the statutory window. Its sole defense of cash flow shortage and financial hardship is explicitly rejected by law as a ground to excuse non-use.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The IPO Director correctly ordered the removal of the mark 'CRISP' from the Register.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 124.2 and 152.1. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: DAU must be filed within 3 years from filing date under Section 124.2 of R.A. 8293.
Failure to file DAU causes removal of the registered mark from the Register.
Under Section 152.1, lack of funds is explicitly excluded as an excuse for non-use of a mark.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Mountain Springs Co. sought to register the word 'ALPINO' for its bottled mineral water. The IPO examiner refused registration on the ground that 'ALPINO' is a descriptive geographical term indicating origin from the Alps. Mountain Springs proved that it had exclusively and continuously used 'ALPINO' in Philippine commerce for over 25 years, spending millions in nationwide promotion, such that the drinking public exclusively associates 'ALPINO' bottled water with Mountain Springs. Can 'ALPINO' be registered as a trademark?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, 'ALPINO' can be registered as a trademark under the Doctrine of Secondary Meaning.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 123.1(j) of R.A. 8293, descriptive or geographical terms are generally non-registrable. However, Section 123.2 provides an exception: descriptive signs may be registered if they have become distinctive in relation to the applicant's goods as a result of long and exclusive commercial use in the Philippines (Doctrine of Secondary Meaning). Proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use for 5 years is prima facie evidence of distinctiveness.
suggestedAnswer.application: Although 'ALPINO' is geographically descriptive, Mountain Springs demonstrated continuous, exclusive commercial use in the Philippines for 25 years. This extensive use transformed the descriptive word into an identifier of Mountain Springs' specific bottled water product, satisfying the Doctrine of Secondary Meaning.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Mountain Springs is entitled to register 'ALPINO' as a trademark.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 123.1(j) and 123.2; Ginebra San Miguel, Inc. v. Director of the Bureau of Trademarks, G.R. No. 196372, August 9, 2022. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2022/aug2022/gr_196372_2022.html.

keyPoints: Descriptive and geographical terms are generally non-registrable under Section 123.1(j).
Doctrine of Secondary Meaning under Section 123.2 permits registration when a descriptive term acquires distinctiveness through long, exclusive use.
Five years of substantially exclusive and continuous commercial use in the Philippines creates a prima facie presumption of distinctiveness.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Prima Meats produces processed ham in distinctive red cloth-like pouches featuring a sliced ham illustration. Competitor Delta Meats, which previously sold ham in plain rectangular cardboard boxes, suddenly changed its packaging to identical red cloth-like pouches displaying a substantially similar layout design, while keeping its registered trademark 'DELTA'. Prima Meats sued Delta Meats for trademark infringement and unfair competition. The court found no trademark infringement because the word marks 'PRIMA' and 'DELTA' were visually distinct. Can Delta Meats nonetheless be held liable for unfair competition?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, Delta Meats can be held liable for unfair competition despite the absence of trademark infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 168 of R.A. 8293 and San Miguel Pure Foods Co., Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc. (G.R. Nos. 217781 & 217788), trademark infringement and unfair competition are distinct causes of action. Unfair competition does not require a registered mark or identical word marks; its essential elements are: (1) confusing similarity in the general appearance or get-up of the goods, and (2) intent to deceive the public or defraud a competitor.
suggestedAnswer.application: Delta Meats deliberately switched from plain cardboard boxes to red cloth-like pouches mimicking Prima's overall packaging and visual layout. This creates confusing similarity in general appearance. Intent to deceive is properly inferred from Delta's abrupt adoption of packaging nearly identical to its competitor's established get-up.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Delta Meats is liable for unfair competition.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 168; San Miguel Pure Foods Co., Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc., G.R. Nos. 217781 & 217788, June 20, 2018. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2018/jun2018/gr_217781_2018.html.

keyPoints: Unfair competition under Section 168 focuses on the overall general appearance (get-up) of goods, not registration or word marks.
Liability for unfair competition can exist even if trademark infringement is absent.
Intent to deceive the public may be inferred from copying the overall packaging and layout design.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Titanium Inc. owns the trademark 'TITAN', which is registered in the Philippines for luxury sports cars and internationally recognized as a well-known mark. Heavy Duty Corp. filed an application to register 'TITAN' for industrial cement mixers. Titanium Inc. opposed the registration, claiming protection as a well-known mark. Heavy Duty Corp. countered that sports cars and industrial cement mixers belong to completely different classes and are non-competing. Rule on the opposition.

suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Sections 123.1(f) and 147.2 of R.A. 8293, protection for a mark registered in the Philippines that is established as well-known extends even to goods and services that are NOT similar or related to those covered by the registration, provided: (1) the mark is well-known; (2) use of the mark on the dissimilar goods indicates a connection with the registered owner; and (3) the registered owner's interests are likely to be damaged.
suggestedAnswer.application: Here, 'TITAN' is a registered well-known mark. Using 'TITAN' on heavy machinery creates an impression of sponsorship or commercial connection with the famed luxury vehicle maker, diluting its prestige and causing damage to Titanium Inc.'s brand goodwill.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The opposition should be sustained: the protection of a well-known mark registered in the Philippines extends to goods that are not similar, since the use would indicate a connection with Titanium Inc. and is likely to damage its interests.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 123.1(f) and 147.2. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Registered well-known marks are protected against use on dissimilar or non-competing goods under Sections 123.1(f) & 147.2.
Requisites: well-known status, indication of connection between goods, and likelihood of damage to owner's interest.
Different product classification does not bar protection for a registered well-known mark.

questions.prompt: Engineer Santos designed an innovative automotive engine valve gasket that improves fuel efficiency. He secured copyright registration certificates from the National Library for his technical engineering drawings of the gasket. Six months later, Santos discovered AutoParts Co. manufacturing and selling physical engine valve gaskets identical to his drawings. Santos sued AutoParts Co. for copyright infringement. AutoParts Co. moved to dismiss, contending that functional mechanical parts cannot be protected by copyright. Decide the case.

suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 175 of R.A. 8293 and established jurisprudence (Ching v. Salinas, G.R. No. 161295; Pearl & Dean v. Shoemart, G.R. No. 148222), copyright protection extends only to original literary and artistic expressions, not to functional or utilitarian objects, methods, or industrial designs. Copyright in a technical drawing protects the drawing itself against reproduction as a drawing, but does not grant exclusive rights to manufacture the functional object depicted.
suggestedAnswer.application: Santos' engine valve gasket is a functional automotive component whose aesthetic design cannot be conceptually separated from its utilitarian function. Manufacturing the physical gasket does not infringe the copyright of the technical drawing.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Santos cannot claim copyright infringement over the physical engine valve gaskets.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 175; Ching v. Salinas, G.R. No. 161295, June 29, 2005; Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., G.R. No. 148222, August 15, 2003 (decided under P.D. No. 49). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2005/jun2005/gr_161295_2005.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2003/aug2003/gr_148222_2003.html.

keyPoints: Copyright protects expression, not functional articles or utility methods under Section 175 of R.A. 8293.
Ching v. Salinas holds that functional vehicle parts are not works of applied art and cannot be copyrighted.
Pearl & Dean establishes that copyright in technical drawings does not extend to the manufacture of the physical article depicted.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Mayor Ramos commissioned Maria, an independent professional sculptor, to create a bronze statue of a local hero for the city plaza for P500,000. The written contract was silent regarding copyright ownership. After Maria completed and delivered the statue, the City Government printed and sold souvenir T-shirts displaying photos of the statue. Maria sued the City Government for copyright infringement. The City Government argues that because it commissioned and paid for the work, it owns all rights to the statue. Who owns the copyright?

suggestedAnswer.application: Here, Mayor Ramos commissioned Maria to sculpt the statue. Because their contract contained no written stipulation assigning the copyright to the City Government, ownership of the physical statue transferred to the city, but the copyright stayed with Maria.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Maria owns the copyright, and the City Government's unauthorized reproduction of the statue on commercial T-shirts constitutes copyright infringement.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 178.4; Sec. 181, as amended by R.A. No. 10372. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2013/ra_10372_2013.html.

keyPoints: Under Section 178.4 of R.A. 8293, ownership of a commissioned work is dual: physical object vs copyright.
The commissioning party owns the physical work, while the creator retains the copyright.
Transfer of copyright in a commissioned work requires an express written agreement.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: News Network A obtained exclusive live broadcast footage of an ongoing hostage crisis. News Network B intercepted Network A's live feed and rebroadcast a 15-minute segment of the raw video footage on its own commercial news program without permission or attribution, placing its own station logo over Network A's feed. Network A sued Network B for copyright infringement. Network B raised the defense of fair use for news reporting. Is Network B's fair use defense valid?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, Network B's fair use defense is invalid.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 185 of R.A. 8293, fair use for news reporting is decided by weighing four factors: (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used; and (4) the effect of the use on the potential market for or value of the work. In ABS-CBN Corp. v. Gozon (G.R. No. 195956), the Court held that news footage is protected by copyright, that commercial use weighs against fair use, and that raising fair use does not automatically mean no infringement was committed.
suggestedAnswer.application: Network B used Network A's broadcast for direct commercial news rivalry without attribution. Rebroadcasting a substantial 15-minute chunk of raw exclusive footage directly harms Network A's market value and commercial exclusivity.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Network B committed copyright infringement, and its fair use defense fails.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 185, as amended by R.A. No. 10372; ABS-CBN Corporation v. Gozon, G.R. No. 195956, March 11, 2015. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2013/ra_10372_2013.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2015/mar2015/gr_195956_2015.html.

keyPoints: Fair use is decided by weighing the four factors of Section 185 of R.A. 8293.
ABS-CBN v. Gozon: news footage is copyrightable, and a news-reporting purpose does not by itself make the use fair.
Commercial rebroadcasting of substantial raw video footage impairs market value and negates fair use.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In 2018, renowned painter Fernando sold an original oil painting directly to Art Gallery for P100,000. In 2024, Art Gallery resold the original painting at a public auction to a collector for P2,000,000. Fernando learned of the resale and demanded a 5% share of the gross proceeds (P100,000) based on his statutory resale right. Art Gallery refused, claiming that once Fernando sold the painting, all his rights over the physical artwork were exhausted. Is Fernando entitled to the 5% share?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, Fernando is entitled to the 5% share of the gross resale proceeds.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 200 of R.A. 8293 (Droit de Suite / Resale Right), in every sale or lease of an original work of painting or sculpture or of the original manuscript of a writer or composer, subsequent to the first disposition thereof by the author, the author or his heirs shall have an inalienable right to participate in the gross proceeds of the sale or lease to the extent of five percent (5%). This right exists during the author's lifetime and for 50 years after death.
suggestedAnswer.application: The transaction between Art Gallery and the collector was a subsequent sale of an original oil painting following Fernando's first disposition. Fernando's statutory resale right is inalienable and operates notwithstanding the transfer of physical ownership.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Art Gallery is legally obligated to pay Fernando 5% of the gross resale proceeds (P100,000).

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 200. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Section 200 of R.A. 8293 grants authors an inalienable 5% resale right in gross proceeds of subsequent sales of original paintings, sculptures, or manuscripts.
The resale right persists during the author's lifetime plus 50 years posthumously.
Transfer of physical ownership of the artwork does not extinguish the statutory droit de suite.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: E-Shop, an online e-commerce platform, hosts independent merchants. Merchant X continuously uploads and sells pirated digital PDF copies of copyrighted law textbooks on E-Shop. The copyright owner sent formal written notices to E-Shop specifying the infringing listings. E-Shop ignored the notices, retained the listings, and continued collecting a 10% commission on every sale made by Merchant X. Is E-Shop liable for copyright infringement?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, E-Shop is liable for vicarious copyright infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 216(b) of R.A. 8293 (as amended by R.A. 10372), a person is liable for vicarious copyright infringement if he benefits from the infringing activity of another who commits an infringement, provided the person benefiting has been given notice of the infringing activity and has the right and ability to control the activities of the other person.
suggestedAnswer.application: E-Shop met all three statutory requisites: (1) it received formal written notice of the infringement; (2) it had the right and ability to control its platform listings by taking down merchant listings; and (3) it directly derived financial benefit by earning a 10% commission on every pirated PDF sale.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
E-Shop is vicariously liable for copyright infringement under Section 216(b).

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 216(b), as amended by R.A. No. 10372. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2013/ra_10372_2013.html.

keyPoints: Vicarious copyright infringement under Section 216(b) requires notice, right and ability to control, and direct financial benefit.
Failure of an online platform to remove infringing items after formal notice renders it liable.
Earning commissions from infringing sales satisfies the direct financial benefit element.

questions.prompt: Engr. Castro devised a modified bamboo scaffold connector that dramatically simplifies assembly on construction sites. He applied for a utility model registration with the Intellectual Property Office. The IPO examiner rejected the application on the sole ground that the connector lacked an inventive step because any experienced construction worker could easily deduce the modification. Engr. Castro appealed, arguing that utility models do not require an inventive step to be registrable. Is Engr. Castro's contention legally correct?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, Engr. Castro's contention is legally correct.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 109.1 of R.A. 8293, an invention qualifies for registration as a utility model if it is new and industrially applicable; Section 21 applies to utility models except for its reference to inventive step as a condition of protection.
suggestedAnswer.application: Here, Engr. Castro's modified bamboo connector was rejected solely for lacking an inventive step. Because the statute only mandates novelty and industrial applicability for utility models, the examiner improperly imposed an inventive step requirement that applies exclusively to invention patents.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Therefore, the IPO examiner erred in rejecting the application for lack of an inventive step; that is not a requirement for a utility model.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 109.1. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Utility models require only novelty and industrial applicability under Section 109.1 of R.A. 8293.
An inventive step is NOT a statutory requirement for utility model registration.
Rejection based on lack of an inventive step is legally erroneous.
questions.correction: Correction: The legal basis now follows Sec. 109.1(a) and (b) exactly (Sec. 21 applies to utility models except the inventive-step requirement). NotebookLM's conclusion said the application "should be granted"; it now says only that rejecting it for lack of an inventive step was wrong, since other requirements still apply. Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 109.1.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: PharmaGlobal holds a Philippine patent for a life-saving cardiovascular medication, which it sells locally at P500 per tablet. A local medical foundation purchased authentic packages of the exact same patented medication directly from an authorized distributor in India—where PharmaGlobal lawfully sells it at P50 per tablet—and imported them into the Philippines for affordable distribution to public hospitals. PharmaGlobal sued the foundation for patent infringement, claiming its Philippine patent gives it exclusive distribution rights within the country. Will the infringement suit prosper?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, PharmaGlobal's patent infringement suit will not prosper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 72.1 of R.A. 8293, as amended by R.A. 9502 (the Cheaper Medicines Act), the owner of a patent cannot prevent the use of a patented product put on the market by the owner or with his express consent; and with regard to drugs and medicines, this limitation applies once the drug or medicine has been introduced in the Philippines or anywhere else in the world by the patent owner, or by any party authorized to use the invention. The right to import such drugs and medicines is available to any government agency or any private third party.
suggestedAnswer.application: PharmaGlobal lawfully manufactured and placed the cardiovascular drug on the Indian market through its authorized distributor. By virtue of international exhaustion, PharmaGlobal's patent rights over those specific imported medicine units were exhausted upon their initial lawful sale abroad, allowing parallel importation into the Philippines.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Consequently, the foundation's parallel importation of authentic patented drugs does not constitute patent infringement.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 72.1, as amended by R.A. No. 9502. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2008/ra_9502_2008.html.

keyPoints: Section 72.1 of R.A. 8293 (as amended by R.A. 9502) adopts the doctrine of international exhaustion for drugs and medicines.
For drugs and medicines, patent rights are limited once the drug has been introduced anywhere in the world by the patent owner or by a party authorized to use the invention.
Parallel importation of genuine patented medicines from foreign markets is legal and non-infringing.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM said patent rights end once the drug is sold abroad by the patent owner "or with its express consent". Sec. 72.1 as amended says: introduced anywhere in the world by the patent owner or by any party authorized to use the invention, and the right to import is open to any government agency or private third party. The legal basis and a key point were corrected. Check R.A. No. 9502, Sec. 7 (amending Sec. 72.1).

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Inventor Mateo published a detailed scientific paper describing his newly invented solar cell efficiency controller in an international academic journal on March 1, 2024. Encouraged by positive peer reviews, Mateo filed a patent application for the solar controller with the Philippine IPO on November 15, 2024. The patent examiner cited Mateo's own March 2024 journal article as prior art that destroyed the novelty of his invention. Mateo contends his application is timely under the statutory grace period. Is Mateo's invention patentable?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, Mateo's invention remains novel and patentable.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 25 of R.A. 8293, disclosure of information contained in a patent application shall not prejudice the applicant on the ground of lack of novelty if the disclosure was made during the twelve (12) months preceding the filing date or the priority date of the application, provided the disclosure was made by the inventor himself or by a third party who obtained the information directly or indirectly from the inventor.
suggestedAnswer.application: Mateo published his journal article on March 1, 2024, and filed his Philippine patent application on November 15, 2024—within 8 and a half months. Because the public disclosure was made by the inventor himself within the 12-month grace period, it is non-prejudicial and does not destroy the novelty of his invention.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The examiner erred, and Mateo's invention retains its novelty under Section 25.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 25. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Section 25 of R.A. 8293 provides a 12-month grace period for non-prejudicial public disclosures.
Disclosures made by the inventor within 12 months prior to filing date do not destroy novelty.
Academic publication by the inventor 8.5 months before application filing is protected.
questions.correction: Correction: The legal basis now quotes Sec. 25.1 exactly: the 12 months run back from the filing date or the priority date (NotebookLM mentioned only the filing date). Nothing else changed. Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 25.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A major public health crisis broke out in the Philippines due to a sudden outbreak of a viral respiratory disease. Global Meds owns the sole Philippine patent for the only effective antiviral treatment but refused to grant local licenses or scale up local supply, resulting in severe drug shortages and exorbitant prices. The Secretary of Health requested the Director General of the IPO to issue a compulsory license to a qualified local pharmaceutical manufacturer. Global Meds opposed, claiming compulsory licenses cannot be issued without the patentee's consent. Can the IPO issue a compulsory license over Global Meds' patent?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, the IPO can issue a compulsory license over Global Meds' patent even without its consent.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 93 of R.A. 8293, as amended by R.A. 9502, the Director General of the IPO may grant a license to exploit a patented invention, even without the agreement of the patent owner, in favor of any person who has shown his capability to exploit the invention, on grounds that include: national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency (93.1); where the public interest, in particular health, so requires (93.2); and where the demand for patented drugs and medicines is not being met to an adequate extent and on reasonable terms, as determined by the Secretary of Health (93.6).
suggestedAnswer.application: The viral respiratory outbreak constitutes a national health emergency and public urgency. Global Meds' refusal to license or supply the market at reasonable volume and price directly justifies government intervention via compulsory licensing under R.A. 9502.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The IPO Director General may grant the compulsory license, in favor of a manufacturer that has shown its capability to exploit the invention.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 93.1, 93.2 and 93.6, as amended by R.A. No. 9502. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2008/ra_9502_2008.html.

keyPoints: Compulsory licensing under Section 93 of R.A. 8293 does not require patent owner consent.
National emergency, public health necessity, and extreme urgency are statutory grounds for compulsory licensing.
R.A. 9502 strengthened compulsory licensing powers for public health needs.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM's list of grounds ("public health necessity, non-commercial public use") didn't match the law. The legal basis now gives the grounds in Sec. 93 as amended that fit the facts (93.1 extreme urgency, 93.2 public interest including health, 93.6 unmet demand for medicines as determined by the Secretary of Health), and the conclusion now says the license goes to someone who has shown the capability to exploit the invention. Check R.A. No. 9502, Sec. 10 (amending Sec. 93).

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In 2000, SoftCo registered the mark 'FLUFFY' for synthetic cotton batting. Over the next two decades, the term 'fluffy' became universally used by the general public, trade publications, and competitors as the common generic name for all synthetic batting materials, regardless of manufacturer. SoftCo took no action to police or preserve the distinctiveness of its mark. In 2024, a competitor filed a petition with the IPO to cancel the registration of 'FLUFFY'. SoftCo opposed, arguing that a validly registered trademark can never be canceled once it becomes well-known. Rule on the petition for cancellation.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The petition for cancellation should be granted, and the mark 'FLUFFY' canceled.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 151.1(b) of R.A. 8293, a registered mark may be canceled at any time if it becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it was registered (Doctrine of Genericide). The test is the primary significance of the registered mark to the relevant public, rather than purchaser motivation.
suggestedAnswer.application: SoftCo allowed 'FLUFFY' to lose its trademark significance through widespread, unpoliced generic usage, causing it to become the common descriptive name for synthetic cotton batting in the trade and public mind. Once a mark undergoes genericide, registration can no longer be maintained.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The IPO must cancel the trademark registration for 'FLUFFY'.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 151.1(b). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Section 151.1(b) permits trademark cancellation when a registered mark becomes generic (genericide).
A mark loses trademark protection when it becomes the common descriptive name for a product category.
Failure to police a mark leads to loss of distinctiveness and cancellation.
questions.correction: Correction: Added to the legal basis: the test for genericide is the primary significance of the mark to the relevant public, rather than purchaser motivation. Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 151.1(b).

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Nestle owns the registered trademark 'NAN' for infant milk formula. A local manufacturer filed an application to register the trademark 'NANNY' for its own line of powdered infant milk. Nestle filed an opposition, alleging confusing similarity. The local manufacturer argued that 'NANNY' contains two syllables and extra letters, making it visually distinct from 'NAN'. Is there confusing similarity between the two marks?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, there is confusing similarity between the marks 'NAN' and 'NANNY'.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 123.1(d) of R.A. 8293, a mark cannot be registered if it nearly resembles a registered mark for the same or closely related goods as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion. In Societe des Produits Nestle, S.A. v. Dy (G.R. No. 172276), the Court applied the Dominancy Test, which focuses on the main, prevalent or essential features of the marks, and took into account the aural effects of the words, in holding that 'NANNY' is confusingly similar to 'NAN'.
suggestedAnswer.application: Applying the Dominancy Test and the doctrine of Idem Sonans, 'NANNY' incorporates the entirety of Nestle's dominant mark 'NAN' as its prefix. When spoken in commercial transactions for infant milk, the two marks produce nearly identical sound impressions, creating a high likelihood of consumer confusion.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The opposition must be sustained and the registration of 'NANNY' denied.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 123.1(d); Societe des Produits Nestle, S.A. v. Dy, Jr., G.R. No. 172276, August 8, 2010. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2010/aug2010/gr_172276_2010.html.

keyPoints: Dominancy Test and Idem Sonans rule assess phonetic/aural similarity under Section 123.1(d).
Incorporating an established mark as the dominant prefix creates confusing similarity.
Societe des Produits Nestle v. Dy held 'NANNY' confusingly similar to 'NAN' under the Dominancy Test.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM's legal basis described Nestle v. Dy as an "Idem Sonans rule" case. The Court applied the Dominancy Test (taking the sound of the words into account) and held NANNY confusingly similar to NAN. The legal basis and a key point were rewritten to say that, and the Basis gives the respondent's full name (Dy, Jr.). Check G.R. No. 172276.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: BrandCo owns the registered trademark 'VELOX' for sports footwear. Wanting to raise capital, BrandCo assigned the trademark 'VELOX' to Footwear Inc. under a written contract without transferring its shoe manufacturing factory, machinery, or business goodwill. The assignment was duly recorded with the IPO. Later, a creditor challenged the assignment, claiming that under Philippine law, a trademark assignment is void unless accompanied by the transfer of the entire business enterprise. Is the assignment of the trademark valid?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, the assignment of the trademark 'VELOX' is valid.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 149.1 of R.A. 8293, an application for registration of a mark, or its registration, may be assigned or transferred with or without the transfer of the business using the mark. The assignment must be in writing and signed by the parties (149.3), and it has no effect against third parties until recorded at the IPO (149.5). It is void only if it is liable to mislead the public as to the nature, source, manufacturing process, characteristics or suitability of the goods (149.2).
suggestedAnswer.application: Unlike a trade name, which can change ownership only with the transfer of the enterprise (Section 165.4), a mark may be assigned without the business using it. BrandCo's assignment was in writing and recorded with the IPO, and nothing in the facts shows it would mislead the public, so it is valid and effective against third parties such as the creditor.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The creditor's challenge fails, and the trademark assignment to Footwear Inc. is legally sound.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 149 and 165.4. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Trademarks may be assigned with or without the business enterprise under Section 149.1 of R.A. 8293.
A written assignment has effect against third parties once recorded with the IPO (Section 149.5).
Contrast with trade names, which cannot be assigned independently of the business enterprise.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM said the assignment was valid against third parties "pursuant to Section 149.2"; Sec. 149.2 is the rule that an assignment is void if it would mislead the public. Recording makes it effective against third parties under Sec. 149.5. The legal basis, application and a key point were corrected, and Sec. 165.4 (trade names transfer only with the enterprise) was added. Check R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 149 and 165.4.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Composer Carlos wrote the musical score, and Lyricist Lina wrote the lyrics, for an original musical play entitled 'Himig'. They worked together with the joint intention of combining their contributions into a single unified work. Three years after the play's premiere, Lina individually licensed her lyrics to a textbook publisher to be printed as poetry in a high school literature book, without obtaining Carlos' consent or sharing royalties. Carlos sued Lina for copyright infringement. Is Lina liable for copyright infringement?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, Lina is not liable for copyright infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 178.2 of R.A. 8293, co-authors of a work of joint authorship are the original owners of the copyright, and in the absence of agreement their rights are governed by the rules on co-ownership. If, however, the work consists of parts that can be used separately and the author of each part can be identified, the author of each part is the original owner of the copyright in the part that he has created.
suggestedAnswer.application: The lyrics and the musical score of 'Himig' can be used separately, and each author is identified: Carlos wrote the music and Lina the lyrics. Lina is therefore the owner of the copyright in her lyrics, and licensing her own lyrics to a publisher is an exercise of her own right, not an infringement of Carlos' copyright in the music.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Lina did not infringe Carlos' copyright by licensing her own lyrics.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 178.2. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Co-authors own the copyright in a joint work, governed by co-ownership rules absent agreement (Section 178.2).
Where parts can be used separately and each author is identified, each author owns the copyright in his own part.
Using or licensing one's own separable part is not infringement of the co-author's part.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM's answer said Lina "must account to Carlos for his share of royalties" and may exploit her part "provided it does not prejudice the joint work"; neither is in Sec. 178.2. The answer now says only what the law says: where the parts can be used separately and each author is known, each author owns the copyright in his own part. The answer, all four parts and the key points were rewritten. Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 178.2.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Sculptor Mario created a marble statue and sold all his economic copyright rights to Art Museum Inc. under a formal contract. Two years later, Art Museum Inc. publicly displayed the statue but replaced Mario's engraved signature on the base with the name of a famous donor, and painted bright pink polka dots over the marble surface without Mario's knowledge. Mario filed an action for violation of his moral rights. Art Museum Inc. moved to dismiss, claiming Mario surrendered all rights when he assigned his economic copyright. Decide.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Art Museum Inc.'s motion to dismiss must be denied; Mario's action for moral rights violation will prosper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 193 of R.A. 8293, the author of a work has moral rights independently of the economic rights or of any assignment or license of them, including the right to require that the authorship of the work be attributed to him (193.1) and the right to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of, or other derogatory action in relation to, his work which would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation (193.3). Under Section 198, as amended by R.A. 10372, the right of attribution lasts during the author's lifetime and in perpetuity after his death, the other moral rights are coterminous with the economic rights, and moral rights are not assignable or subject to license.
suggestedAnswer.application: Removing Mario's name violates his statutory right of attribution (Section 193.1), and painting polka dots over the marble sculpture distorts his artistic creation, infringing his right to object to prejudicial modification (Section 193.3). Selling economic rights does not strip Mario of these moral protections.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Art Museum Inc. is liable for violating Mario's moral rights under Section 193.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 193; Sec. 198, as amended by R.A. No. 10372. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2013/ra_10372_2013.html.

keyPoints: Moral rights under Section 193 of R.A. 8293 are independent of economic rights and survive assignment.
Right of attribution prohibits removing or altering the author's name on the work.
Right of integrity allows the author to object to prejudicial distortion or mutilation.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM said moral rights last for the author's life and 50 years and called the right to object to changes Sec. 193.2. Under Sec. 198 as amended in 2013, the right to be named as author lasts forever, the other moral rights last as long as the economic rights, and none can be assigned; the right to object to prejudicial changes is Sec. 193.3 (193.2 is the right to alter or withhold before publication). Check R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 193, and R.A. No. 10372, Sec. 17.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: SoftWare Store purchased 100 legitimate boxed retail copies of an OS operating system software. SoftWare Store set up a commercial rental business renting out these physical software installation discs to computer repair shops for P200 per day. SoftWare Store contends that under the first sale doctrine, purchasing authentic physical copies exhausted the copyright owner's distribution rights, allowing unrestricted rental. The software developer sued SoftWare Store for copyright infringement. Who is correct?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The software developer is correct; SoftWare Store is liable for copyright infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 177.4 of R.A. 8293, the copyright owner has the exclusive right to carry out, authorize or prevent the rental of the original or a copy of, among others, an audiovisual or cinematographic work, a work embodied in a sound recording, or a computer program, irrespective of the ownership of the original or the copy which is the subject of the rental. By contrast, the distribution right in Section 177.3 covers only the first public distribution of each copy.
suggestedAnswer.application: While the first sale doctrine exhausts general resale rights for physical goods, Section 177.4 creates an explicit statutory exception for computer software and audiovisual works. Commercial rental of standalone software without the copyright owner's consent violates exclusive rental rights.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
SoftWare Store committed copyright infringement by engaging in unauthorized commercial rental.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 177.3 and 177.4. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Section 177.4 of R.A. 8293 grants exclusive commercial rental rights over computer programs and audiovisual works.
Commercial rental rights survive the first sale of genuine software copies.
Unauthorized commercial rental of software constitutes copyright infringement.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM's legal basis said Sec. 177.4 applies "where the program itself is the essential object of the rental"; that phrase isn't in the law. It now quotes what Sec. 177.4 says (rental of computer programs and other works "irrespective of the ownership" of the copy) and contrasts it with Sec. 177.3. Check R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 177.3 and 177.4.

questions.prompt: Singer Clara performed a live acoustic concert at a private auditorium. suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 203 of R.A. 8293, performers enjoy exclusive rights (neighboring rights) independent of songwriter copyrights. Specifically, Section 203.1 grants performers the exclusive right to authorize the broadcasting, communication to the public, and fixation of their live performances.
suggestedAnswer.application: Radio Station XYZ recorded and broadcast Clara's live acoustic performance without her authorization. Although Clara did not compose the underlying songs, her live performance is independently protected under Section 203.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Radio Station XYZ violated Clara's performers' rights, making it liable for damages.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 203.1. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Performers enjoy independent neighboring rights under Section 203 of R.A. 8293.
Broadcasting or fixating live performances without performer consent is prohibited.
Performers' rights exist independently of underlying song copyright ownership.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: TechCorp (a foreign franchisor) entered into a licensing agreement with LocalCo (a Philippine licensee) for patented food processing technology. Clause A of the contract prohibited LocalCo from exporting the processed food products outside the Philippines, while Clause B required LocalCo to purchase all raw packaging materials exclusively from TechCorp's designated overseas supplier at fixed prices. LocalCo challenged these clauses before the IPO Documentation, Information and Technology Transfer Bureau (DITTB). Are Clauses A and B enforceable?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, Clauses A and B are prohibited technology transfer terms and are unenforceable.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 87 of R.A. 8293, except in the exceptional cases under Section 91, certain clauses in technology transfer arrangements are deemed prima facie to have an adverse effect on competition and trade, including those that oblige the licensee to acquire raw materials and other goods from a specific source (87.1), and those that prohibit the licensee from exporting the licensed product unless justified to protect the licensor's legitimate interest, such as exports to countries where exclusive licenses have already been granted (87.8). Under Section 92, non-conformance with Sections 87 and 88 automatically renders the technology transfer arrangement unenforceable, unless it is approved and registered with the Documentation, Information and Technology Transfer Bureau under Section 91.
suggestedAnswer.application: Clause A bars LocalCo from exporting, with nothing in the facts showing a legitimate interest such as exclusive licenses already granted abroad. Clause B forces LocalCo to buy its raw packaging materials from a specific source. Both are prohibited clauses under Section 87, and the arrangement has not been approved as an exceptional case under Section 91.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Clauses A and B are prohibited, and their inclusion renders the technology transfer arrangement unenforceable under Section 92 unless it is approved and registered with the DITTB under Section 91.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 87.1, 87.8, 91 and 92. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Section 87 of R.A. 8293 lists clauses deemed prima facie adverse to competition and trade.
Requiring purchases from a specific source (87.1) and unjustified export bans (87.8) are prohibited clauses.
Under Section 92, such clauses render the arrangement unenforceable unless approved under Section 91.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM cited Secs. 88.3 and 88.5 for the prohibited clauses and Sec. 89 for unenforceability. In the IP Code, prohibited clauses are Sec. 87 (87.1 buying from a specific source, 87.8 export bans), Sec. 88 lists mandatory clauses, Sec. 89 is about the licensor's rights, and unenforceability is Sec. 92. The legal basis, application, conclusion and key points were rewritten. Check R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 87, 91 and 92.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Luzon Weavers manufactures handwoven shawls in Laguna using synthetic thread. To boost sales, Luzon Weavers attached labels stating 'Authentic Handwoven Yakan Tapestry - Made in Basilan, Mindanao' onto every shawl, capitalizing on the high reputation of indigenous Yakan weavers. Luzon Weavers did not copy any registered trademark. Indigenous Yakan weaving cooperatives sued Luzon Weavers for unfair competition under the IP Code. Luzon Weavers defended that unfair competition requires copying a registered trademark. Rule on the defense.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Luzon Weavers' defense is invalid; it is liable for unfair competition.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 168.1 of R.A. 8293, a person who has identified his goods in the mind of the public has a property right in that goodwill whether or not a registered mark is employed, and passing off one's goods as those of the one who established that goodwill is unfair competition (168.2). Separately, Section 169.1(b) makes liable to a civil action for damages and injunction any person who, in commercial advertising or promotion, uses a false designation of origin or misrepresents the geographic origin of his goods.
suggestedAnswer.application: Luzon Weavers labeled synthetic shawls made in Laguna as authentic Yakan tapestries made in Basilan, riding on the goodwill of Yakan weavers. Neither unfair competition nor a false designation of origin requires copying a registered trademark: the label itself misrepresents the goods' geographic origin and source.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The defense fails: no registered mark is needed, and the false label makes Luzon Weavers liable under the IP Code's rules on unfair competition and false designation of origin (Sections 168 and 169.1).

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 168.1, 168.2 and 169.1(b). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html.

keyPoints: Unfair competition protects goodwill whether or not a registered mark is employed (Section 168.1).
Section 169.1(b) gives a civil action against false designations or misrepresentations of geographic origin.
Copying a registered trademark is not required for either.
questions.correction: Correction: NotebookLM cited Sec. 168.3(c) for false designation of geographic origin; Sec. 168.3(c) is about false statements that discredit another's goods. False designation of origin is Sec. 169.1(b), and Sec. 168.1 protects goodwill "whether or not a registered mark is employed". The legal basis, application, conclusion and key points were rewritten. Check R.A. No. 8293, Secs. 168 and 169.1.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: University Library owned a single fragile copy of a rare out-of-print 1920 historical monograph. To prevent complete physical loss, the library, which is not run for profit, made one photocopy of it to keep in its collection for reference, since copies are no longer available from the publisher. suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 188.1 of R.A. 8293, as amended by R.A. 10372, a library or archive whose activities are not for profit may, without the authorization of the author or copyright owner, make a limited number of copies of a work by reprographic reproduction, as may be necessary to fulfill its mandate, where (a) the work by reason of its fragile character or rarity cannot be lent to users in its original form, or (c) the copy is made to preserve and, if necessary, replace a copy, and copies are not available with the publisher.
suggestedAnswer.application: University Library is not run for profit; the monograph is rare and fragile, and copies are no longer available from the publisher. Making a photocopy to preserve it and keep it available for reference falls within Section 188.1.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The reproduction is permitted under Section 188.1, so the library is not liable.

**Basis:** R.A. No. 8293, Sec. 188.1, as amended by R.A. No. 10372. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1997/ra_8293_1997.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2013/ra_10372_2013.html.

keyPoints: Non-profit libraries and archives may make limited reprographic copies without the owner's authorization (Section 188.1).

questions.prompt: What is the legal effect if a trademark registrant does not display a notice of registration, such as the words "Registered Mark" or the letter R in a circle, with the mark?

questions.explanation:
The two blanks are "original" and "creation": a work must be an original intellectual creation, and it is protected from the moment it is created. Section 172.2 adds that works are protected by the sole fact of their creation, whatever their mode or form of expression, content, quality or purpose.
